# Notes-1 — SQ1 (Cagan's position, verbatim) and SQ3 (role vs activity/accountability wording)

Gathered 2026-08-25. "Opened in full" = raw HTML downloaded with curl and article body extracted; quotes copied from the extracted text. Ellipses inside quotes are mine; nothing else altered.

## A. Cagan / SVPG — primary

### 1. Cagan, "Product Manager vs. Product Owner" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-manager-vs-product-owner/ — opened in full.
- "All too often I run into companies that have resigned themselves to having two different people covering the product role."
- "Usually the way they split it is they have one person responsible for interacting with customers and stakeholders (which they often call the product manager), and another to interact with the development team and manage the backlog (which they usually call the product owner)."
- "There are many “product managers” that are not technical enough to effectively engage with the developers, yet management hopes to utilize them.  And there are many “product owners” that show no inclination or ability to get out of the building and interact with customers, yet management knows this is critical."
- "I have written earlier that this approach has two common negative consequences.  This first is that there is no clear owner (neither person takes responsibility for the product), and the second is a common lack of respect or understanding between the two (the “product manager” doesn’t appreciate the technical complexities, and the “product owner” doesn’t appreciate the customer’s pain)."
- "In order to make the many hundreds of large and small decisions a product owner makes every week, he needs to have deep understanding of the customers.  Deep customer knowledge is what informs the decisions.  It is actually the main thing a capable product owner brings to the party and it is what distinguishes him from the others on the team."
- "Similarly, when interacting with customers and identifying problems and opportunities, it is the knowledge of the technology and what is possible that informs the discussions and the potential solutions.  This is what distinguishes a product person from other roles such as marketing, user research or sales, and why it’s essential that the product person has the direct customer interaction."
- "I know this doesn’t make it any easier to find people that are willing and able to do both, but I do hope that more company leaders come to understand how essential it is to find product people that can cover both aspects of the role."
Note: Cagan's argument here is about *one person* ("two different people covering the product role"), and he speaks of "both aspects of the role" — i.e. one role with two aspects.

### 2. Cagan, "Product Manager vs. Product Owner Revisited" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-manager-vs-product-owner-revisited/ — opened in full.
- "Five years ago I wrote an article arguing that it is essential that the product manager is also the product owner.  My motivation, which I made no secret of, was that I was worried about this point because more than a few companies were using the relatively new role of the product owner as an excuse to once again separate “the business person” from the “the person that talks with the developers.”"
- "Starting about a decade ago, there were many people calling themselves “product owners,” and rather than add another person to the team, I was fine just treating “product manager” and “product owner” largely synonymously.   I didn’t really care what the person was called, so long as it was one person."
- "Nothing wrong with that if they just realized that this prepared them only for the Agile rituals the product owner has to perform, but for many, that’s not what happened. For many product owners, they actually thought this meant they were trained as product managers."
- "I wanted to remind people what a product manager is actually responsible for, and how the product owner responsibility is just a very minor part."
- "So going forward, I promise to be more rigorous about this.  If you tell me you’re the product manager, I’ll double check that you’re also the product owner, but if you tell me that you are the “product owner” then I will ask you if you are also the product manager?  Are you just administering the backlog, or are you actually tackling and solving difficult problems for your customers and your business?"
Note (SQ3): Cagan's vocabulary shifts within this essay — "role of the product owner", "product owner responsibility", "Agile rituals the product owner has to perform". The PO is treated as a responsibility/ritual-set held by the PM, and the operative test is "one person".

### 3. Cagan, "Product Management – Start Here" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-management-start-here/ — opened in full.
- "If your engineers are using Agile methods for delivery, then there’s an important administrative role called the product owner, and the product manager needs to cover these responsibilities."
- "The key is to understand that the product owner responsibilities are just a very small subset of the product manager responsibilities.  And now you may be starting to understand why there are so many ineffective product managers."
- "As product manager, you’re responsible for ensuring that what gets built is both valuable and viable." (returned by WebFetch of the same page; consistent with the essay's framing)
Note (SQ3): Cagan here calls the PO an "administrative role" and, in the same sentence, a set of "responsibilities" the PM "needs to cover" — role and responsibility-subset used interchangeably.

### 4. Cagan, "Two in a Box PM" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/two-in-a-box-pm/ — opened in full.
- "One of the few things both groups generally agree on is that however you define the job, it’s often too much work for one person. Hence the very understandable desire to cut the role up, and split it among two or more different people."
- "I will tell you up front that in a great many situations I see, the way the job is defined indeed really is too much for one person. ... But the way the job is scoped down is the key, and unfortunately, the most common ways of trimming down the role have consequences far worse than most companies realize."
- "In order for the product manager to be effective in addressing value and viability, there are a few things that are absolutely critical, and these are what you need to be very careful about preserving as you go about scoping down the role: Direct Access To Users and Customers ... Direct Access to Business Stakeholders ... Direct Access to Engineers and Designer"
- "What this means is that you need to protect the product manager’s direct access to these three constituencies, and fight any temptation to place a person (or process) between the PM and these people. It is in fact the direct, ongoing access to these three constituencies that enables the product manager to make good decisions regarding value and viability."
- "Cutting up the PM job to have a product manager that interacts with customers and stakeholders, but a different person (e.g. product owner) that interacts with the engineers, causes the PM to lose the direct access to engineers."
- "When I refer to the two-in-a-box PM anti-pattern, it is referring to splitting up responsibility for these three constituencies among two different people.  There are many ways this happens, but in my experience, this is a very serious mistake leading to long-term negative consequences."
- (On what *may* be offloaded) "Now it’s important to note that it’s normal for the PM to be responsible for acceptance testing, but that is a very minor responsibility compared to the much larger quality assurance role." and, on research admin: "I strongly encourage the organization to get some part-time administrative help to support this work."
Note: This is Cagan's most precise statement of *why* one person: the harm is loss of direct access to customers/stakeholders/engineers, not the existence of a second role as such. He explicitly sanctions offloading administrative load (research logistics, QA) while keeping the PM's access intact — a "one accountability, helpers for admin" shape.

### 5. Cagan, "The Product Manager Contribution" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/the-product-manager-contribution/ — opened in full.
- "That said, most teams know and acknowledge that the product manager is the product owner (another very unfortunate choice of word) in the Agile sense, and as such, the main deliverable they are responsible for is the backlog (what the team will build).  However, to some the backlog may appear as a simple list of user stories.  It can look like just a few minutes work, where the hard part is determining what to build."
- "It is absolutely possible that the technology lead or the product designer is sometimes capable of covering the role of the product manager as well, and there are some real advantages to this, but most people, once they understand what’s really required, usually back off of trying to cover two roles themselves because of the volume of work."
- "First, this entire discussion assumes an empowered product team.  If we’re talking a feature team, the role is very different and is essentially a project management role."

### 6. Cagan, "Behind Every Great Product" (SVPG, revised essay)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/behind-every-great-product/ — opened in full.
- "They usually have the title “product manager” but they might be a startup co-founder or the CEO, or they might be in another role on the team and stepped up because they saw the need.  The title is not important; the work they do is."
- "In this model, the product manager is really a backlog administrator.  Lots of CEO’s tell me this is the model they’re in and it’s not working.  If you think the product manager job is what’s described in a Certified Scrum Product Owner class, you almost certainly fall into this category."
- "Product Management is absolutely distinct from the other disciplines. ... The role I would argue that the product manager is most similar to is the role of the CEO.  But with the obvious difference that unlike the CEO, nobody reports to the product manager."

### 7. Cagan, "Product Managers vs. Business Owners" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-managers-vs-business-owners/ — opened in full.
- "Be careful not to confuse the concept of a business owner with a ‘product owner’ which is the term used in Scrum teams for the product manager role."
- "Things go wrong when these two roles are not clearly defined, especially when the business owner believes he is responsible for the product solutions."
- "So if your company has a central product organization trying to meet the needs of multiple business units, you¹ll need to make very clear to everyone involved on the business side and the product side what the roles and responsibilities are ..."
Note: Cagan does accept a *second, differently-scoped* role beside the PM (business owner) provided its responsibilities are explicit and it does not own solutions — a useful contrast to his PO position.

### 8. Cagan, "A Fresh Definition of The Product Role" (SVPG)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/a-fresh-definition-of-the-product-role/ — opened in full.
- "I’m just guessing here, but I’d say over the years I’ve seen at least one hundred different definitions of the product role (i.e. product manager/product owner)."
- "Part of the problem is that there are different operating models that require different responsibilities and skills from the person playing the product role."
Note (SQ3): "product role (i.e. product manager/product owner)" — the two names are treated as one role; "person playing the product role" — role is something played.

### 9. Cagan interview, Mark A. Jansen, "An interview about EMPOWERED with Marty Cagan" (LinkedIn)
URL: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/interview-empowered-marty-cagan-mark-a-jansen — opened via WebFetch (tool-extracted quotes; page not downloaded in full by me).
- "The job title is Product Manager. The role the product manager plays on an Agile team is the product owner role."
- "many people would go to a short and simple CSPO training, and come out of that understandably considering themselves product owners."
- "It's the same problem as if we were to send engineers to Scrum training and think that after a few hours they are trained in computer science as software developers."
Note (SQ3): This is the cleanest Cagan statement of the shape: PM = job title; PO = a role the PM plays within the Agile process.

### 10. Cagan Q&A with Stefan Wolpers, "Marty Cagan on the Product Operating Model and Scrum" (Age-of-Product)
URL: https://age-of-product.com/marty-cagan-product-operating-model/ — opened in full.
- "Marty Cagan: Most “scrum teams” are just sets of developers with a backlog administrator product owner, also known as a “delivery team.” An empowered product team is a fully cross-functional set of professionals – developers, designer, and product manager ... More generally, Scrum is a particular delivery process. A product team is designed for both discovery and delivery, and the engineers can use whatever delivery process they consider most appropriate for the delivery task at hand."
- "Marty Cagan: A product owner is roughly 10% of a true product manager. Your “scrum team” is completely missing a professional product designer. A scrum master is a role normally played by the delivery manager ..."
- "To be blunt, a Scrum team is quite amateur compared to a professional product team."

### Unopened / not usable
- Mind the Product, "The role of a product manager — Marty Cagan (Part 2)" https://www.mindtheproduct.com/the-role-of-a-product-manager-marty-cagan/ — page opened but contains only the episode blurb; no transcript. Nothing quoted.
- Lenny's Newsletter, "Product management theater | Marty Cagan" https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/product-management-theater-marty — page opened but transcript body not present in the HTML (only timestamps/links). Nothing quoted. Episode blurb (site copy, not Cagan verbatim): "“fake” product managers engage in non-essential activities, often under titles like Agile coaches, product owners, product operations, or business analysts."
- O'Reilly, INSPIRED 2nd ed. ch.10 https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/inspired-2nd-edition/9781119387503/c10.xhtml — HTTP 403; unopened. Book excerpt on "the product owner role should be something the PM does" therefore NOT verified from the book; the SVPG essays above carry the same claim.

## B. Scrum Guide 2020 — primary

### 11. Schwaber & Sutherland, The Scrum Guide (November 2020)
URL: https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html — opened in full.
- "The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers. Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies."
- "The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint. Scrum defines three specific accountabilities within the Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master."
- "The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. How this is done may vary widely across organizations, Scrum Teams, and individuals."
- "The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal; Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items; Ordering Product Backlog items; and, Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood."
- "The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable."
- "For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review."

## D. Cross-source observations (for the synthesis)

1. Vocabulary by source (SQ3):
   - Cagan: PO is variously "an important administrative role", "the product owner responsibilities ... a very small subset of the product manager responsibilities", "the Agile rituals the product owner has to perform", "the term used in Scrum teams for the product manager role", and (interview) "The role the product manager plays on an Agile team is the product owner role." Title = PM; PO = role/ritual-set played by the PM. Operative test: "so long as it was one person."
   - Scrum Guide 2020: no "role" word; PO is an *accountability* held by "one person, not a committee"; the *work* "may delegate ... to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable." Accountability is singular and non-delegable; execution is delegable.
   - Pichler: "the product owner is a product management role"; "you can think of the product owner as an agile product manager"; SAFe's strategic/tactical split is "a common scaling technique" but naming the tactical role PO is "an unfortunate mistake"; "what truly matters are not our job titles and role names."
2. Agreement: all three agree PO and PM should not be two people with the PM outward-facing and the PO inward/backlog-facing at the level of *accountability*; all three accept that *work* may be shared or delegated (Cagan: research admin, QA, business owner; Scrum Guide: delegation clause; Pichler: feature/component owners, "ownership has to be shared" post-PMF).
3. Conflict: Pichler explicitly disagrees with Cagan's characterisation of the PO ("based on how he has seen the role applied rather than how it is intended"); Cagan calls the PO "roughly 10% of a true product manager" and "a backlog administrator"; Pichler says the Scrum PO has "full-stack product ownership" and is "more than just a re-branded product manager" (PO = PM + x, 2010). They agree on one person, disagree on which name carries the larger scope.
4. Cagan's *reason* for one person (Two in a Box) is stated as preservation of direct access to three constituencies (customers/users, stakeholders, engineers/designer), and loss of a single owner. He does not argue against a second role as such; he argues against any split that interposes "a person (or process) between the PM and these people."
5. Cagan's own definition of what the PM is accountable for: "ensuring that what gets built is both valuable and viable"; the PM-as-PO "main deliverable ... is the backlog (what the team will build)."
6. Milner (Mountain Goat) notes the residual gap in the Scrum Guide's move: "accountability" names the duties, but the thing that bundles several accountabilities into "one Product Owner" is still, functionally, a role — relevant to a system that defines roles as capability contracts.

- "Additionally, SAFe uses a product owner role which is different from the Scrum product owner. The latter has full-stack product ownership: The individual owns all aspects of a product, the vision, strategy, and tactics. But the SAFe product owner owns only the tactical product decisions and hence has partial ownership. ... Splitting product ownership in this way is a common scaling technique. But calling the tactical role “product owner,” as SAFe does, is an unfortunate mistake: Having two product owner roles with different levels of authority and responsibility creates confusion and gives rise to misunderstandings."
- "Note that I have always viewed the Scrum product owner as an agile product manager. I would hence not agree with the notion that the product manager role is only outward-facing and strategic in nature."
- "An early version of Scrum did, in fact, use the product manager role. In a paper presented at the OOPSLA conference in 1995, Ken Schwaber ... used the term product manager. [2] Subsequently, the name was changed to product owner, though."
- "By offering the product owner role, these organisations can start working in an agile way without first having to establish a product management group and initiate an organisational change process. Instead, employees from the appropriate business units can—with some training and coaching—act as product owners."
- "Last but not least, the term product owner strengthens the idea that the person in charge of the product must be empowered and respected. ... If no agreement can be reached, the product owner makes the necessary decision thereby avoiding a deadlock ..."
- "In the short run, we should acknowledge that the product owner is a product management role. People playing the role should therefore acquire the relevant product management skills."
- "Additionally, I recommend using either the term product manager or product owner in your company and qualifying it, for instance, by employing the terms senior and junior product manager or junior and senior product owner. This reduces confusion and helps unite people."
- Reply in comments: "Hi Madison, As I explain in the article, there is no product manager in Scrum. You can think of the Scrum product owner as the agile product manager."
- Reply in comments: "Secondly, review the split between strategic product people (“product managers”) and tactical folks (“product owner”). If the spilt works well, great, but consider renaming the “product owners” to tactical product manager/person."

URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/six-types-of-product-owners/ — opened in full.
- "As its name suggests, a product owner in Scrum is in charge of a product. Note that the choice of the name is intentional. It is also not called “product manager” primarily to indicate the level of empowerment and respect product owners require to succeed in their jobs. But you can think of the product owner as an agile product manager ..."
- "the SAFe model splits product ownership into two distinct roles: The SAFe product manager owns the strategic product decisions, and the SAFe product owner is in charge of the tactics. This is in stark contrast to the Scrum product owner who exercises full-stack product ownership, from vision to tactics ..."
- "As long as you search for a valid strategy to launch a product, achieve product-market fit, and then keep the product growing, it is particularly important to dovetail strategic and tactical product decisions. - "Each of the roles above is a product management role; anybody playing one of the roles takes on product ownership ... But as indicated, the ownership scope significantly differs and with it, the empowerment and skills required to succeed."

URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/product-owner-product-manager/ — opened in full.

The following formula captures this insight: Product Owner = Product Manager + x"

- Pichler reply (2013): "Scrum has the concept of a *single* product owner, which I find useful at least until product market fit has been achieved. But when the product grows, ownership has to be shared ..."

### 18. Pichler, "How Agile Has Changed Product Management"
URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/how-agile-has-changed-product-management/ — opened in full.
- "When coining the Scrum terms, Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland chose the term product owner instead of product manager in order to emphasise the level of authority and empowerment a product person requires—especially in an agile context where collaboration is valued, and stakeholders and dev teams regularly contribute to product decisions."

### Pichler, podcast "Product Manager vs. Product Owner"
URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/podcast/product-manager-vs-product-owner/ — opened; page holds only the blurb (same as blog intro); no transcript. Nothing further quoted.

## D. Cross-source observations (for the synthesis)

1. Vocabulary by source (SQ3):
   - Cagan: PO is variously "an important administrative role", "the product owner responsibilities ... a very small subset of the product manager responsibilities", "the Agile rituals the product owner has to perform", "the term used in Scrum teams for the product manager role", and (interview) "The role the product manager plays on an Agile team is the product owner role." Title = PM; PO = role/ritual-set played by the PM. Operative test: "so long as it was one person."
   - Scrum Guide 2020: no "role" word; PO is an *accountability* held by "one person, not a committee"; the *work* "may delegate ... to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable." Accountability is singular and non-delegable; execution is delegable.
   - Pichler: "the product owner is a product management role"; "you can think of the product owner as an agile product manager"; SAFe's strategic/tactical split is "a common scaling technique" but naming the tactical role PO is "an unfortunate mistake"; "what truly matters are not our job titles and role names."
2. Agreement: all three agree PO and PM should not be two people with the PM outward-facing and the PO inward/backlog-facing at the level of *accountability*; all three accept that *work* may be shared or delegated (Cagan: research admin, QA, business owner; Scrum Guide: delegation clause; Pichler: feature/component owners, "ownership has to be shared" post-PMF).
3. Conflict: Pichler explicitly disagrees with Cagan's characterisation of the PO ("based on how he has seen the role applied rather than how it is intended"); Cagan calls the PO "roughly 10% of a true product manager" and "a backlog administrator"; Pichler says the Scrum PO has "full-stack product ownership" and is "more than just a re-branded product manager" (PO = PM + x, 2010). 4. Cagan's *reason* for one person (Two in a Box) is stated as preservation of direct access to three constituencies (customers/users, stakeholders, engineers/designer), and loss of a single owner. 5. Cagan's own definition of what the PM is accountable for: "ensuring that what gets built is both valuable and viable"; the PM-as-PO "main deliverable ... is the backlog (what the team will build)."
6. Milner (Mountain Goat) notes the residual gap in the Scrum Guide's move: "accountability" names the duties, but the thing that bundles several accountabilities into "one Product Owner" is still, functionally, a role — relevant to a system that defines roles as capability contracts.

# SQ2 notes — the case FOR two distinct PM and PO roles, and reported consequences of split vs combined

Gathered 2026-08-25. Every quote is verbatim from a page opened in this session unless marked otherwise. Access status per source: opened in full / abstract only / could not be opened. Nothing below is from memory.

Summary of what the sources actually show (details and quotes follow):

- The strongest *principled* case for two roles comes from SAFe (scale: "a single person cannot handle product and market strategy while also being dedicated to agile teams"), Pichler's scaling essay (strategic/tactical split "works well if a tight integration ... is not required"), Pragmatic Institute (PM owns pricing, ROI, portfolio; PO is a subset; distributed teams need a local PO) and Product Focus (survey: 35% of PMs also do the PO role at ~40% of their time; "get someone else to do the Product Owner role – someone who takes direction from you").
- The strongest *empirical* evidence of consequences of splitting is Remta & Buchalcevová (SAFe case study + activity mapping): when PM and PO are split SAFe-style, "the PO's accountability for product leadership fades away" and "real Product Ownership lies in the hands of the Product Manager." Perri reports the same from training SAFe teams: "I have never seen this work well ... No one is doing validation work."
- The academic scaling literature (Bass & Haxby; Sverrisdottir et al.; Paasivaara et al.) shows that at scale the single PO is tailored into a *product owner team* or split business/technical, i.e. splitting is a reported practice, but these papers describe activities and do not report outcome comparisons of split vs combined.
- Scrum.org (Dave West) and LeSS are the counterweight: one decision-maker; the PO "should be performed by a business person, and for many organizations that means a product manager."
- No source found offers controlled or quantitative evidence comparing outcomes of split vs combined roles. Verwijs (2020) explicitly: "There is unfortunately a lack of quantitative research in this field."

---

## 1. Roman Pichler — "Product Manager vs. Product Owner"
URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/product-manager-vs-product-owner/
Status: opened in full (via WebFetch; article published 2017-03-14, last updated 2023-01-13).
Position: one product-management role; PO is an agile PM. Argues against SAFe's two-tier arrangement.

Quotes:
- "the product owner role originated in Scrum, where it is responsible for 'maximising the value of the product'"
- "Scrum as a simple framework focused on helping teams develop complex products. It is not a product management framework."
- "the Scrum product owner as an agile product manager. I would hence not agree with the notion that the product manager role is only outward-facing."
- "the SAFe product owner owns only the tactical product decisions and hence has partial ownership" while "the SAFe product manager...makes the strategic product decisions."
- "Having two product owner roles with different levels of authority and responsibility creates confusion and gives rise to misunderstandings."
- "the product owner is a product management role. People playing the role should therefore acquire the relevant product management skills."
- "I recommend using either the term product manager or product owner in your company and qualifying it...This reduces confusion and helps unite people."

Note: WebFetch returned the passages with some ellipses; the wording within each quoted fragment is verbatim.

## 2. Roman Pichler — "Scaling the Product Owner Role"
URL: https://www.romanpichler.com/blog/scaling-the-product-owner/
Status: opened in full (WebFetch; published 2016-06-28).
Position: the strongest *conditional* case for a strategic/tactical split, with named risks.

Quotes:
- "In theory, the product owner is one person. But in practice, managing a larger, complex product is usually a shared effort."
- "Young products tend to require a significant amount of experimentation and rework...Having a single product owner in place supports this."
- "Once the product is becoming more successful and start growing...a single person can usually no longer manage the product."
- "The initial product owner should be in charge of the overall product, take care of the product strategy and roadmap...still be involved in managing the product backlog."
- "Feature and component owners manage their assets: they capture new ideas and requirements, test them using feedback and data."
- "The strategic role is sometimes called product manager and the tactical one is referred to as product owner."
- "Splitting product responsibilities along the strategic-tactical dimension works well if a tight integration...is not required."
- "If you use this scaling option at an earlier life cycle stage, then you face the risk of strategic decisions not effectively guiding tactical ones."
- "Tactical insights...not informing the strategic decisions, particularly when several people take on tactical duties."
- "You should not rely on one scaling technique. Instead, consider the life cycle stage of your product."

Consequence claims (Pichler): the strategic/tactical split risks (a) strategy not guiding tactics, (b) tactical learning not feeding strategy; it is fit for mature products where tight integration is not required, and unfit for young products that need experimentation.

## 3. Scrum.org / Dave West — "Product Owner vs. Product Manager"
URL: https://www.scrum.org/resources/product-owner-vs-product-manager
Status: opened in full (page is JS-rendered; WebFetch and curl returned empty; retrieved via r.jina.ai reader proxy; dated December 22, 2016, by Dave West).
Position: counterpoint — one decision-maker; PO should be the product manager.

Quotes:
- "As a Product Owner and the CEO of Scrum.org I was invited to speak at ProductTank NYC earlier this year about the conflict between the roles Product Owner and Product Manager. And how organizations need to consolidate on one overall decision maker for the product, and that person should be engaged with the delivery teams as a representative of the business / customer."
- "Scrum is very clear, there can only be one Product Owner. By having a single individual responsible for the product, that doesn't mean they do all of the work, the Product Owner role removes a lot of inefficiencies that exist with group ownership."
- "The Product Owner however is not all knowing, if you find that person who knows all, hire them as it is very rare. That is why they will rely on people like business analysts, product managers, etc. to help them with understanding the product direction and what needs to be delivered."
- "The best Scrum Teams have a Product Owner that is available and empowered to make decisions without having to ask for permission. That means that the Product Owner role should be performed by a business person, and for many organizations that means a product manager."
- "Yes, this means more work for the product manager, who is often already drowning in a sea of external and internal requests, but if that person wants the right product delivered they MUST directly support the delivery team. This requires leadership, not doing all of the tasks that are required to build a great product, but instead empower and work with others in both the business and Scrum Development Team to do the work."

Note: "Who is the Product Owner Anyway?" (https://www.scrum.org/resources/who-product-owner-anyway, 2017-04-18, West & van Lanen webinar) opened via the same proxy; it is a webinar abstract only, with one relevant line: "for many organizations there is some 'confusion' with existing roles of business analyst, product manager or even project manager." No Verwijs or Wolpers article titled "PO is/isn't a PM" was found on Scrum.org; see items 9 and 10 for what they do say.

## 4. SAFe — Product Owner page
URL: https://framework.scaledagile.com/product-owner
Status: partially opened — login-walled; only the summary section is visible (WebFetch reports "The full article content beyond the summary section requires authentication").
Position: two roles by design; PO is team-level, "part of the larger Product Management function".

Quotes (from the visible summary):
- "The Product Owner (PO) is the Agile team member primarily responsible for maximizing the value delivered by the team"
- "The PO is the 'voice of the customer' on the AgileTeam, representing the needs of end-users and the business."
- "Together with Product Management, they ensure that product strategy and implementation remain connected across teams."
- "Each PO acts as a bridge between an Agile Team and its customers."
- "They are part of the larger Product Management function and maintain alignment with the Solution Vision"

## 5. SAFe — Product Management page
URL: https://framework.scaledagile.com/product-management
Status: partially opened — login-walled; summary only.

Quotes (from the visible summary):
- "Product Management is the function responsible for defining desirable, viable, feasible, and sustainable solutions that meet customer needs"
- "They manage and prioritize the ART backlog, collaborate with cross-functional teams"
- "Product Managers usually fulfill this function."
- "More than one Product Manager may be needed for a single ART, which happens often when an ART contains multiple products or complex systems"

Note: the visible portion does not state the PM/PO split rationale; that rationale is quoted secondhand through Remta & Buchalcevová (item 11), who cite SAFe's own text: "SAFe implies that a single person cannot handle product and market strategy while also being dedicated to agile teams."

## 6. Pragmatic Institute — "Product Owner vs Product Manager: What's the difference?"
URL: https://www.pragmaticinstitute.com/resources/articles/product/product-owner-vs-product-manager-whats-the-difference/
Status: opened in full (WebFetch; no author/date on page). (The URL .../product-manager-vs-product-owner/ is 404.)
Position: two roles in larger organisations; one person in small ones; hybrid when constrained.

Quotes:
- "The lines between the roles are blurred in some organizations and nonexistent in others, as one role carries the responsibilities of both."
- "The Product Manager focuses on the overall strategy behind a product and the Product Owner handles the tactical, day-to-day management of the product development process."
- "Product Managers establish the 'why' behind the product. Product Owners establish the 'how' it gets done."
- "In larger organizations or companies developing complex products, both roles are necessary to manage the product's lifecycle effectively."
- "Startups or smaller teams with more straightforward products may have a single person fill both roles."
- "The decision depends on many factors, like the company's size, structure, and the product's complexity and development process."

## 7. Pragmatic Institute — "The Strategic Role of Product Management (When Development Goes Agile)"
URL: https://www.pragmaticinstitute.com/resources/articles/product/the-strategic-role-of-product-management-when-development-goes-agile/
Status: opened in full (WebFetch; no author/date extracted).
Position: PO is a subset of PM; a separate PO is warranted only by distribution; co-located teams need none.

Quotes:
- "Product owner and product manager are not the same. In fact, a product owner's responsibilities are just a small subset of product management."
- "As you can see, the role of product management includes the responsibilities of product owner—plus much more."
- "Real revenue is driven by pricing and packaging. Product managers typically own pricing; product owners rarely do."
- "The point of integration for these teams, though, is a single product manager. When the executives demand 'one throat to choke,' it's the product manager who is responsible for overall success."
- "Good product managers look across the product line for ways to make the overall collection more valuable. Hermetically-sealed product teams tend toward local optimization."
- "One agile product manager can handle all of the demands from a product team that sits together...When everyone sits together, there's no need for a product owner."
- "When Development is split across time zones and continents, one product manager can't possibly provide the face-to-face daily input and leadership that agile development demands...Having someone in each office responsible for keeping the team clear on user stories/backlogs seems essential."
- "It is common for product owners to report to the development organization, but product managers are increasingly reporting into their own department—separate from Development and from Marketing."

## 8. Product Focus (Ian Lunn) — "A Product Owner is not a Product Manager" (survey data)
URL: https://www.productfocus.com/a-product-owner-is-not-a-product-manager/
Status: opened in full (WebFetch; no date on page).
Position: two roles; PM owns the product; delegate PO to someone who takes direction from the PM. Only survey figures found in this sweep.

Quotes:
- "A Product Owner is a role defined by the Scrum Agile methodology...The focus is on optimizing development and working with the Development team."
- "So if anyone owns the product within the business it's the Product Manager. It's not the person managing the requirements – the Scrum 'Product Owner'."
- "According to our annual survey, 35% of Product Managers also do the Product Owner role."
- "It seems to average out at just under 2 days a week. That's 40% of a Product Managers' time attending meetings with Development and working on requirements."
- "It is another role to take on and means you've got less time for everything else."
- "Our preference is to try and get someone else to do the Product Owner role – someone who takes direction from you. Maybe a Business Analyst or Manager working in Development."

Caveat: survey year, sample and method are not stated on the page; the underlying survey report was not opened.

## 19. Mike Cottmeyer / LeadingAgile — "Product Owner vs Product Manager" (2009-02)
URL: https://www.leadingagile.com/2009/02/product-owner-vs-product-manager/ (site now liminalarc.co)
Status: opened in full (via r.jina.ai proxy).
Position: the Scrum PO is an *abstraction* of many traditional roles, of which PM is one; the abstraction breaks down at scale.

Quotes:
- "Most teams start with the assumption that the Product Owner role should be filled by the Product Manager. I think that is a reasonable starting point"
- "When you look at all the things an agile Product Owner is doing for the team you see pretty quickly that the role of Product Owner is really much, much more than that of a traditional Product Manager."
- "it is my premise that in Scrum, the Product Owner either has the responsibility for, or is an abstraction of, every other role not previously accounted for in discussing the ScrumMaster and the Team. The Product Owner is the Project Manager, the Business Analyst, the System Designer, the User Experience Architect, and every other Business Group... all rolled into one."
- "I know there are many teams out there with Project Managers and UI Designers and Analysts that probably think they are doing Scrum just fine. ... I bet they are assuming additional coordination and communication costs to make it happen."
- Reply in comments (Cottmeyer): "that view of product management doesn't scale past a single product with a single team."

---

## Conflicts and gaps

1. Ownership location. SAFe (as described by Remta & Buchalcevová) and Product Focus put real product ownership with the PM and make the PO a delegate; Scrum.org (West) and LeSS put it with the single PO and say that person should *be* the product manager. Pichler agrees with West/LeSS on principle but allows a strategic/tactical split for mature products. Pragmatic Institute allows either, keyed to organisation size and distribution.
2. Consequence claims disagree on direction: Pragmatic/Product Focus/SAFe argue the split protects strategy time and gives distributed teams local ownership; Perri, Pichler (scaling essay), and Remta & Buchalcevová report the split disconnects the PO from customers, breaks the strategy-to-tactics feedback loop, and hollows out PO accountability ("fades away").
3. Evidence quality: no quantitative or controlled comparison of split vs combined roles was found. Product Focus's "35% / ~40% of time" is the only survey figure, with method unstated. Academic sources are case studies (Remta: 3 interviews; Bass & Haxby: 93 interviews but descriptive of activities, not outcomes; Sverrisdottir: small Icelandic interview set, abstract only). Verwijs states the gap explicitly.
4. Terminology: Bass & Haxby's "product owner team" and Sverrisdottir's "two product owners (business/technical)" are splits *within* product ownership, not PM-vs-PO splits; they support "one accountability, several execution positions" more than "two roles".

- Paasivaara et al. 2012 (DOI 10.1109/ICGSE.2012.41) — metadata only.
- Unger-Windeler et al. 2021 (DOI 10.1002/smr.2311) and 2018 (arXiv:1809.00830) — 403 / not opened.
- "Clarifying the Role of Product Owners: A Comprehensive Taxonomy" (DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-92826-0_4, 2025) — Springer page failed to load.
- "The Product Owner and its Impact on Success and Challenges in Agile Scrum Projects: An Interview Study" (ScienceDirect S1877050924015254) — captcha.
- Bass, "How product owner teams scale agile methods to large distributed enterprises," Empirical Software Engineering — cited in item 13, not opened.
- Pragmatic Institute "Cage Fight: Product Owner vs. Product Manager" webinar and podcast — not opened.

- "it is my premise that in Scrum, the Product Owner either has the responsibility for, or is an abstraction of, every other role not previously accounted for in discussing the ScrumMaster and the Team. The Product Owner is the Project Manager, the Business Analyst, the System Designer, the User Experience Architect, and every other Business Group... all rolled into one."

---

## Conflicts and gaps

1. Ownership location. SAFe (as described by Remta & Buchalcevová) and Product Focus put real product ownership with the PM and make the PO a delegate; Scrum.org (West) and LeSS put it with the single PO and say that person should *be* the product manager. Pichler agrees with West/LeSS on principle but allows a strategic/tactical split for mature products. Pragmatic Institute allows either, keyed to organisation size and distribution.
2. Consequence claims disagree on direction: Pragmatic/Product Focus/SAFe argue the split protects strategy time and gives distributed teams local ownership; Perri, Pichler (scaling essay), and Remta & Buchalcevová report the split disconnects the PO from customers, breaks the strategy-to-tactics feedback loop, and hollows out PO accountability ("fades away").
3. Evidence quality: no quantitative or controlled comparison of split vs combined roles was found. Product Focus's "35% / ~40% of time" is the only survey figure, with method unstated. Academic sources are case studies (Remta: 3 interviews; Bass & Haxby: 93 interviews but descriptive of activities, not outcomes; Sverrisdottir: small Icelandic interview set, abstract only). Verwijs states the gap explicitly.
4. Terminology: Bass & Haxby's "product owner team" and Sverrisdottir's "two product owners (business/technical)" are splits *within* product ownership, not PM-vs-PO splits; they support "one accountability, several execution positions" more than "two roles".

Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable. entire organization must respect their decisions. --- 304:As a Product Owner and the CEO of Scrum.org I was invited to speak at ProductTank NYC earlier this year about the conflict between the roles Product Owner and Product Manager. And how organizations need to consolidate on one overall decision maker for the product, and that person should be engaged with the delivery teams as a representative of the business / customer. 316:The best Scrum Teams have a Product Owner that is available and empowered to make decisions without having to ask for permission. That means that the Product Owner role should be performed by a business person, and for many organizations that means a product manager. Yes, this means more work for the product manager, who is often already drowning in a sea of external and internal requests, but if that person wants the right product delivered they MUST directly support the delivery team. This requires leadership, not doing all of the tasks that are required to build a great product, but instead empower and work with others in both the business and Scrum Development Team to do the work. The Product Owner concentrates on defining the right product while the Scrum Development Team concentrates on building the product right.

**Abstract:** "Agentic AI marks a new phase of enterprise automation. # Paper Information

**Title:** "The Role of the Product Owner in Scrum-comparison between Theory and Practices"

**Authors:** Hrafnhildur Sif Sverrisdottir, H. Ingason, H. Jonasson

**Year:** 2014

**Abstract:** "New methods have emerged in last* decades for managing projects and develop software. The agile ideology was generally defined with the agile manifesto in 2001 and is widely used for software project management. Scrum is the most common method within agile and has become one of the most popular tools in software development in Iceland. The objective of this research was to shed light on how Scrum is applied. The role of the product owner is studied; the knowledge and skills he is required to have, according to the Scrum method. This is compared to the perception of a number of actual project owners of their role. Information was gathered by semi structured interviews with a limited number of product owners that have had that role for at least 1 year. The results show that the majority of the participants in the survey are using different project management methods. They apply the methods that best fit their own operations. The understanding of the role and responsibility of the product owner is quite different between organizations but seldom in perfect conformance with the official Scrum method. Cases were reported where there are two product owners for the same product. One is then responsible for business aspect but the other is responsible for technical aspects of the product. Scrum has a strong position in software development with its defined roles, collaboration emphasis, understanding, visibility, effective process and fast development."

content.content:
# Scrum Team Accountabilities

According to the Scrum Guide, "Scrum defines three specific accountabilities within the Scrum Team: the Developers, the Product Owner, and the Scrum Master."

## Product Owner Authority

The Product Owner holds singular decision-making power. The guide emphasizes that this role is "one person, not a committee" and notes the "entire organization must respect their decisions."

Regarding delegation, the framework clarifies an important distinction: "The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable."

This design ensures clear ownership while allowing flexibility in how responsibilities are executed. Even when delegating specific tasks, ultimate accountability for Product Backlog management and value maximization stays with the Product Owner role.

The company’s strategy specifies the goals and objectives to be achieved as well as the values and missions to be pursued; it sets out the basic direction of the company. The strategy specifically delineates the products or services to be provided, the markets to be served, and the value to be offered to the customer. It also specifies sources of competitive advantage. Traditionally, strategy is the first component of the Star Model™ to be addressed. It is important in the organization design process because it establishes the criteria for choosing among alternative organizational forms. (See the book, Designing Dynamic Organizations by Galbraith, Downey and Kates, published by Jossey-Bass in 2002, for tools to help translate strategy into criteria.) Each organizational form enables some activities to be performed well, often at the expense of other activities. Choosing organizational alternatives inevitably involves making trade-offs. Strategy dictates which activities are most necessary, thereby providing the basis for making the best trade-offs in the organization design. Matrix organizations result when two or more activities must be accomplished without hindering the other. Rather than choosing the “or,” matrix requires an embracing of the “and.” Companies want to be global and local. Structure The structure of the organization determines the placement of power and authority in the organization. Structure policies fall into four areas: • Specialization • Shape • Distribution of power • Departmentalization Specialization refers to the type and numbers of job specialties used in performing the work. Large numbers of people in each department create flat organization structures with few levels. Distribution of power, in its vertical dimension, refers to the classic issues of centralization or decentralization. In its lateral dimension, it refers to the movement of power to the department dealing directly with the issues critical to its mission. # Verification review 1 — pm-po-one-role-2026-08 draft

**Method.** Every direct quote in F1–F6 and summary items 1–6 was checked against the gather notes and against the source reopened this session: SVPG essays, Scrum Guide, InfoQ, Milner, Pichler (three essays), Wolpers Q&A from the cached raw HTML; LinkedIn interview, Remta 2020 (Springer via r.jina.ai), Remta & Buchalcevová 2021 (MDPI via r.jina.ai), Bass & Haxby PDF, ISO 24765 PDF, Koch & Wellbrock PDF, Galbraith PDF, Mintzberg scan, Wikipedia (SoD, RACI, maker-checker), Holacracy 5.0, SFIA, Team Topologies, Anthropic, EU AI Act art. 14, Pragmatic, Product Focus, Pichler scaling, LeSS, West, Verwijs, Perri, Sverrisdottir abstract (Semantic Scholar API) refetched live. PDFs were text-extracted locally and grepped.

**Spot-checks named in the brief — all confirmed verbatim and correctly attributed:**
- "so long as it was one person" is on svpg.com/product-manager-vs-product-owner-revisited: "I didn't really care what the person was called, so long as it was one person."
- LinkedIn "An interview about EMPOWERED with Marty Cagan" (Mark A. Jansen) exists; Cagan says "The job title is Product Manager. The role the product manager plays on an Agile team is the product owner role."
- Remta, Doležel & Buchalcevová 2020: "Therefore, the PO's accountability for product leadership fades away." Single case, three semi-structured interviews; interviewee quote confirmed.
- Remta & Buchalcevová 2021: "In SAFe, the real Product Ownership lies in the hands of the Product Manager."; "seems only to be responsible for driving and overseeing the execution of requirements defined in the Product Manager's features."; "SAFe implies that a single person cannot handle product and market strategy while also being dedicated to agile teams."
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765:2010 3.2603 role, def. 2: "a defined function to be performed by a project team member, such as testing, filing, inspecting, coding"; 3.53 activity: "set of cohesive tasks of a process".
- Bass & Haxby 2018: "Product sponsors surround themselves with a product owner team and delegate to a named product owner (see intermediary, below). However, we found that product sponsors maintain focus on the project vision by reviewing important demonstrations"; "the purpose of the intermediary is to be more accessible and available to other project stakeholders than product sponsors."
- Every other quote in F1–F6 (Scrum Guide, InfoQ, Milner, Pichler incl. the comment-reply on Cagan, West, LeSS, Perri incl. "Product Manager is the job.", Verwijs, Pragmatic, Product Focus, Pichler scaling, Sverrisdottir, SoD incl. compensating-controls sentence, RACI, maker-checker, Holacracy, SFIA, Galbraith, Team Topologies, Koch & Wellbrock incl. the anti-pattern row, Anthropic, EU AI Act 14(4)(d), Wolpers "roughly 10%", all SVPG passages) confirmed in the reopened source.
- "seat"/"surface": absent. Confidence and likelihood: never combined; no likelihood phrases appear. Confidence labels reproducible under the stated scheme (F6 medium is defensible). Items 7–8 add no unsourced factual claim and do not misstate 1–6.

**verdict: findings** — all are attribution/labelling corrections; no quote is fabricated, misworded, or from an unopened source; nothing needs retraction or UNVERIFIED.

1. **Executive summary item 3** — "The 2020 Scrum Guide replaced 'role' with 'accountability' precisely so a role would not be read as a job title". scrumguides.org/revisions.html gives no such rationale; it comes only from Milner's secondary commentary, hedged: "Apparently some people thought that the term 'role' meant job title." The InfoQ Q&A gives a different rationale (removing the separate Development Team). Required: attribute to Milner and drop "precisely".

2. **F4, first bullet** — labels the 2021 quote "conclusion:". It is in the Discussion section; the Conclusions section reads "In fact, the Product Manager has real product ownership, while the Product Owner is responsible for driving and overseeing the implementation of the requirements." Required: relabel "discussion:" or quote the Conclusions wording.

3. **F3, ISO bullet and summary item 3** — the quoted role definition is definition 2 of three, credited by the standard to "A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) — Fourth Edition", not to ISO 12207/15288. Required: add "(def. 2, credited to the PMBOK Guide 4th ed.)".

4. **F5, Mintzberg bullet** — "every division of labour requires one of five coordinating mechanisms" is the gather worker's gloss. Source: "Organizational structuring, of course, focuses on the division of labor ... and then the coordination of all of these tasks ... The literature suggests that this coordination can be effected in at least five basic ways". Required: reword to the source's "at least five basic ways" framing; the mechanism list itself is verbatim.

5. **F4 and F5 headings** — bare "*(high / medium)*" does not say which claim carries which label; the summary does. Required: copy the split into the headings ("high that the sources say so; medium on the consequence" / "high for the grounds; medium for Bass & Haxby's pattern").

6. **F2, LeSS bullet** — "The fake PO... can cause damage" is verbatim ("The fake PO is not only not the best Product Owner but also she can cause damage trying to fill a role for which she is not qualified.") but is said of an interim PO during LeSS adoption, not of a PM/PO split. Required: add that context or drop the quote; "connector, not an intermediary" carries the point alone.
